messages.subject: Release of seewave 2.0.1
messages.body_plain:
Dear seewave users,

A new version of seewave (2.0.1) has been pushed to CRAN right now. The
version of each OS should be available soon.

This release is rather important with, in particular, the introduction
of the mel scale, the implementation of the acoustic diversity indices
AR and M, and the improvement of env() and hilbert() through fftw.

I would like to warmly thank Laurent Lellouch, Marion Depraetere, Jean
Marchal and Francois Fabianek for their contribution.

Laurent Lellouch did in particular a great work as testified in the
following (long) list of changes.

Enjoy and have a nice summer or winter depending where you are coding.

Jerome

NEW FUNCTIONS
o AR(): a new function to compute the Acoustic Richness index
(contribution of M. Depraetere)
o combfilter(): a new function to apply a frequency comb filter.
o drawfilter(): a new function to draw interactively the frequency
response of a filter (by Laurent Lellouch).
o M(): a new function to compute the amplitude index (contribution of M.
Depraetere).
o squarefilter(): a new function to generate the frequency response of a
square filter (by Laurent Lellouch).

NEW ARGUMENTS
o corspec(), cutspec(), diffspec(), diffcumspec(), fbands(), fpeaks(),
ks.dist(), localpeaks(), Q(), simspec(), specprop(): a new argument
'mel' to deal with (htk-)mel scale. By Laurent Lellouch.
o diffspec(), simspec(): a new argument 'title'.
o discrets(): a new argument 'plateau' to control how a plateau is
encoded. By Laurent Lellouch.
o env(): a new argument 'fftw' to speed up the computation of the
Hilbert amplitude envelope and/or kernell smoothing through the use of
the package fftw. By Jean Marchal and Francois Fabianek.
o hilbert(): a new argument 'fftw' to speed up the computation of the
Hilbert transform through the use of the package fftw. By Jean Marchal
and Francois Fabianek.
o itakura.dist(), logspec.dist(): a new argument 'scale' to ensure that
the distances are not influenced by the length of the spectra to be
compared. By Laurent Lellouch.
o oscillo(): a new argument 'nidentify' to control the number of
identified points on the wave.
o simspec(): two new arguments, 'norm' and 'PMF', to scale the spectra
between 0 and 1 or transform them into probability mass functions.
o timer(): a new argument 'dmin' to detect signal events above a minimum
duration (time threshold).

OTHER CHANGES
o The dependency with fftw is removed. This should facilitate
installation on different OSs.
o seewave now imports the base packages graphics, grDevices, stats,
utils to comply with new packages check rules.
o cutspec(): a small frequency shift fixed.
o diffspec(): the arguments 'lty1', 'lty2' and 'lty3' have been merged
into a single argument 'lty'; the arguments 'col1', 'col2' and 'cold'
have been merged into a single argument 'col'.
o ks.dist(): the distance 'D' can now be computed even if the sampling
frequency is not provided. By Laurent Lellouch.
o listen(): a bug regarding audioSample objects fixed.
o oscillo(): a bug regarding title fixed.
o oscilloST(): now manages stereo objects of class Wave or audioSample.
o pulse() is renamed pulsew() to avoid confusion with tuneR::pulse.
o Q(): is now faster. By Laurent Lellouch.
o 'rev.cm.colors()', 'rev.gray.colors.1()', 'rev.gray.colors.2()',
'rev.heat.colors()', 'rev.terrain.colors()', 'rev.topo.colors()' have
been renamed 'reverse.cm.colors()', 'reverse.gray.colors.1()',
'reverse.gray.colors.2()', 'reverse.heat.colors()',
'reverse.terrain.colors()', 'reverse.topo.colors()' respectively to
comply with new packages check rules.
o sh(): a new option 'simpson' for the argument 'alpha' to compute the
Simpson (or Gini-Simpson) entropy (index). The Renyi entropy was also
modified to obtain values between 0 and 1. By Laurent Lellouch.
o simspec(): the arguments 'lty1', 'lty2' and 'lty3' have been merged in
to a single argument 'lty'; the arguments 'col1', 'col2' and 'col3' have
been merged in to a single argument 'col'.
o synth(): the length of the arguments 'am' and 'fm' increase to 3 and 4
respectively to add a phase component. By Laurent Lellouch.
o timer(): a bug regarding the argument 'tlim' fixed, a new value
'first' that specifies whether the first event detected is a signal or a
pause.

DEPRECATED & DEFUNCT
o diffspec(): the argument 'dB' is removed has the 'dB' results are not
optimal.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Gianni,

I'm not sure about some of your questions, but I've had success using the package "snowfall" for parallel processing in R. There may be other, more efficient packages out there, but snowfall is a wrapper for the 'snow' package, and I really like how easy it is to use. Essentially you just write a function that does what you want it to do and pass that to snowfall.

I have my function load the audio file, process it, save the output to disk. You can set the number of cpus snowfall should use (useful if you're running this overnight vs. at the same time as doing other work). I also find it useful to have the output of each audio file written to disk independently to avoid cpu's trying to write to the same file at the same time. You can also have your function return the output to snowfall and then wait for snowfall to finish, but I prefer writing to disk. This way, if something glitches or if you need to get your computer back, you can kill the process without losing the work it has already done. It's easy to then to have R read and combine the files together.

I have run into problem with my system load getting usually high, but it could be that my system had other issues or that I didn't write a very efficient code :)

Good luck!

Steffi

Thank you Stefanie for your input regarding parallelisation, something
I have no experience with. The memory issue is really a problem and I
fully understand that waiting so much time to get these indices is not

of both functions) is:
Depraetere M, Pavoine S, Jiguet F, Gasc A, Duvail S, Sueur J (2012)
Monitoring animal diversity using acoustic indices: implementation in
a temperate woodland. Ecological Indicators, 13, 46-54. The pdf is
here:
http://ecoacoustics.perso.sfr.fr/WebPage_PapersPDF/Depraetereetal_EcolIndic_2011.pdf

Best

Jerome

messages.subject_clean: how to get help in R and in seewave
messages.body_plain:
Hi Gianni

You have several solutions to get help.

In R :
(1) help.start()                                 # opens the complete help in your favourite web browser including the help of the packages you have installed
(2) apropos("test")                           # returns a list of functions which name includes the word "test"
(3) ??test                                          # returns a list of functions which name, title, or definition include the word "test"
(4) ?t.test                                         # opens the help of the function t.test. So regarding AR, you can run directly ?AR
(5) vignette(package = "seewave")   # lists the seewave vignettes (= tutorials)
     vignette("seewave_analysis")       # opens in your favourite pdf viewer the vignette named "seewave_analaysis"
     vignette("seewave_IO")                # opens in your favourite pdf viewer the vignette named "seewave_analaysis"

Out of R:
(1) The seewave webpage <http://rug.mnhn.fr/seewave/> offers a thematic list of the functions. Check the 'Documentation' tab. I just added two sections for the alpha and beta indices respectively.
(2) The vignettes and the manual are available here <http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/seewave/index.html> (see Vignettes).
(3) This discussion list!

HTH!

Jerome

> > > > > >

messages.subject: Calibrated SPL values from meanspec()
messages.body_plain:
I am trying to get calibrated SPL values along the frequency spectrum from ambient noise recordings and I ran into several issues on the way to that... probably due to my lack of knowledge in physics.

I am using meanspec() with a mono recording at 44100Hz. First I ran this:
meanspec(sound.mono,f=freq,dBref= 2*10e-5,dB="max0",wl=128)

Which gave me a graph I can't show because picture insertion is still a mess in Google groups (on Light and Firefox), so it is here:
http://imgur.com/nLTr7YB

I am wondering: why do we have to supply a value for dB when we choose that dBref=2*10e-5? When choosing db="max0", dB values do not max out at zero anyway.
Why is it that whenever we call meanspec() with norm=TRUE, the maximum dB seems to be 73.98 dB? What is this magical value?

But now the really important stuff: I am trying to get calibrated SPL values in dB and I am following Merchant et al. 2015 <http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/enhanced/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12330/>. Here is an extract from the supplementary information:

> 3.2 Background
> The general form of the calibration procedure converts the uncorrected signal, b,
> into a calibrated sound level, a, via a correction factor, S:
> a = b − S (1)
> Here, we describe how S can be measured and/or calculated. Fig. 4 shows the
> signal path and conversely the calibration sequence for a typical PAM recorder,
> which helps to contextualise the equations presented below.
 [...]
> Finally, the correction factor can also be computed directly from the system
> specifications, though this is the least reliable of the three methods described here.
> The specifications required are: the transducer sensitivity, Mh(f), in dB re 1 V/µPa;
> the system gain, G(f), in dB, at the frequency of interest, which describes any preamplifier gain applied to the signal; and the zero-to-peak voltage, VADC, of the
> analogue-to-digital converter (ADC). The correction factor, S(f), is then
>
> S(f) = Mh(f) + G(f) + 20log10  VADC 1  + 20log10(2Nbit−1) (4)
>
> where Nbit is the bit-depth of the digital signal (e.g. 16, 24). Note that some software (e.g. MATLAB) normalises the amplitude to ±1 when loading digital audio
> files, though the native format contains integers in the amplitude range −2Nbit−1
> to 2Nbit−1 − 1. If such normalisation has been applied to the digital signal, the final
> term in Eq. 4 is omitted.

So my aim is to find the value "b", the uncalibrated sound level in dB, and then correct it by subtracting "S" (that I have calculated from the manufacturer specifications), to get "a", the calibrated SPL value that could then be compared to anyone's calibrated SPL values.

When we set norm=FALSE in spectro(), the SPL values are in dB (normalized to the mysterious value of 73.98). When we do that in meanspec(), we get linear amplitude values. If I am not missing something there is an incoherence here since we expect the same results as both functions are based on the same FFT function and the argument norm is described identically?

Nevertheless, it should be possible to simply transform the un-normalized, linear amplitude values we get with meanspec() (when norm=FALSE). This is what they look like:
http://imgur.com/Qzbpt3J

So what I did was to transform these linear values using sound pressure level's definition formula:
20*log10(linearvalues/20)=SPL [dB] (assuming we have micropascal here)

I thought that the linear values output by meanspec could be:
- either simple amplitude readings between -2^15 and 2^15 (I record in 16 bit), but actually they are positive?
- or they are actual pressure values (so I could use the previous formula)?

So the question is: how do I transform the linear values output by meanspec() to get uncalibrated SPL values?

messages.body_plain:
So after some research I am trying to answer my own question here.

Although uncommon amon terrestrial ecologists, calibrating sound pressure level (SPL) values will prove to be invaluable to make studies of eco-acousticians comparable, so I hope we will make some progress in this discussion... and it would be awesome if seewave() provided the tools to do that in an uncomplicated way.

It seems that when meanspec(norm=F) is set, the output values are DFT, discrete Fourier Transform values. Not the amplitude, not the pressure.

However meanspec() behaves differently from spectro() in that when normalization is turned off, one cannot supply a dBref value (in spectro() you can).

So to get unnormalized SPL values from meanspec(), I transformed the DFT values:

20*log10(DFTvalues/dBref)

correct?

Indeed this gives me dB values from meanspec() which are close to these output from spectro() for the same file (averaged over time), but not identical. So I am still a bit confused... anyone help?

Moreover, in Merchant et al. 2015, an additional correction term of is applied to the amplitude:
> B is the noise power bandwidth of the window function, which corrects for the energy added through spectral leakage. For the Hann window, B=1.5 (see Harris (1978) for other windows)

in that formula

20*log10(DFTvalues/B*dBref)

Should we do that too?

-calculate fpeaks for all your successive recordings
-plot your results along a time scale (representing your recording times)

I would suggest a loop that first detect your frequential peaks using
fpeaks(), then you can consider the other frequency as zero (so put
zero for each of your frequency not detected by fpeak) and then,
create a matrix with your frequency in row and recording in column,
use the function rbind() to simply paste your frequency vectors in
each column of the matrix). You should now be able to plot this matrix
as a spectogram and be able to design this function as you like (look
into the code of spectro to reproduce the plot parameters that you like)

Hope this help!

Amandine

Dear seewave users,

A new version of seewave (2.0.2) has been pushed to CRAN right now. The
version of each OS should be available soon.

This is a small update with very few changes, listed below.

Enjoy your summer recordings,

Jerome

NEW FUNCTIONS
o duration(): a new function to get the duration (in s) of a time wave.

o ffilter(): a tiny bug fixed, default value of the arguments 'from' and
'to' are now 'NULL' ('FALSE' previously).
o spectro(): the argument 'trel' now works when 'osc=TRUE'.
o synth(): the argument 'signal' accepts now 'sawtooth'.
o timer(): now works even if irrelevant values are provided for the
argument 'dmin'.
